The study "Reflective Writing of New Graduate Students: Their Challenges and Experiences in an Open and Distance Education" by Queenie R. Ridulme and Rachel Anne Joyce C. Sales investigates the transition of first-year graduate nursing students into an open and distance learning (ODL) environment at an open university in the Philippines. Using a qualitative research design guided by Gibbs’ Reflective Cycle, the researchers collected data from 13 graduate nursing students via an online self-administered questionnaire.

The findings revealed a dichotomy of experiences. On the positive side, students valued the flexibility of studying at their own pace and from their workplaces, which fostered independence and responsibility. Many participants noted the ability to apply theoretical knowledge to their actual clinical practice, while support from professors and peers and the satisfaction of achieving high grades served as significant motivators.

Conversely, the study identified significant challenges. The most prominent issue was delayed feedback, which caused confusion and tension. Technical difficulties, including poor internet connectivity, power interruptions, and software errors, also emerged as major barriers. Furthermore, students struggled with time management while balancing work, social life, and academic responsibilities.

The authors recommend that instructors provide more frequent and timely feedback and establish clear guidelines for response times. They also advocate for the continuous enhancement of learning tools, regular updating of modules, and ongoing training for faculty in educational technology.
40:
Queenie Roxas-Ridulme’s study investigates computer self-efficacy (CSE) and attitudes toward e-learning among 33 Master of Arts in Nursing (MAN) students at the University of the Philippines Open University. Using an online survey, the research analyzed how these students perceive their computer abilities and their views on online learning environments.

The findings indicate that students possess high computer self-efficacy at a "beginning" level, though they rated "fairly" in the "advanced" category. While confident in basic tasks like moving a cursor, they showed lower confidence in complex tasks such as troubleshooting hardware or software. Additionally, these students do not extensively use the Internet for educational research, potentially because they are in a non-computer-related discipline.

Regarding attitudes, students demonstrated a highly positive view of e-learning, yielding a total mean score of 4.01. They perceive e-learning as a useful, efficient, and flexible tool for continuing education that facilitates communication and offers equal opportunities for different personality types.

Statistical analysis revealed no significant relationship between computer self-efficacy and attitudes toward e-learning (p-value = 0.902), suggesting that a positive attitude does not depend on a student's level of computer confidence. The researcher recommends encouraging students to use academic databases more extensively and suggests implementing e-counselling to support students facing study difficulties.
